concept.name: Contango
concept.definition: A market situation in which prices in succeeding delivery months are progressively higher than in the nearest delivery month, i.e. the futures curve slopes upward. For physically delivered contracts, contango typically reflects storage, financing, and insurance costs of carrying the commodity; it is the opposite of backwardation.
concept.intuition: The further out in time you buy delivery, the more you pay — because someone has to store, finance, and insure the goods until then.
concept.mechanics: Measured by comparing contract months: F(t, T2) > F(t, T1) for T2 > T1. Physically delivered futures may sit in contango because of fundamental factors like storage, financing (cost to carry), and insurance; the curve can move between contango and backwardation as expectations and inventories change.
concept.formula: Contango condition: F(t, T2) > F(t, T1) for T2 > T1; often summarized by the calendar spread F(t, T2) - F(t, T1) > 0.
concept.failure_modes: Contango describes curve shape, not direction of future prices; spot prices can rise strongly while the curve stays in contango. Persistent deep contango imposes negative roll yield on passive long futures positions, which can dominate returns even when the spot price is flat.
concept.misconceptions: Contango is not a prediction that prices will rise; nor does it make the market 'abnormal' — it is the typical state for storable commodities with positive carrying costs. The opposite of contango is backwardation, not a 'normal market' in the Keynesian sense (normal backwardation is a separate, contested hypothesis).
concept.example: Gold quoted at $360.00 per ounce for January and $355.00 for June would be backwardation; the reverse — January $360 and June $365 — is contango, with the $5 difference approximating five months of financing and storage.

citations.source: CFTC Futures Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
CME Group, CME Institute: What is Contango and Backwardation
